results.notes:
This is the historical contract notice (CN) data reported by Australian Government
agencies for the years 1999 to 2020. The CN data has been sourced from
the Gazette Publishing System (GaPS) for the years 1999 to 2006-07, inclusive,
and from the AusTender from 1 July 2007 onwards.

Effective 1 July 2007, mandatory contract reporting was transferred to
AusTender [www.tenders.gov.au](http://www.tenders.gov.au/) . Notices of
contracts that were active at 1 July 2007 were migrated to AusTender and will
therefore appear in both databases. These records are identifiable on
AusTender by the GaPS ID reference. The reporting requirements for GaPS differed from those for AusTender reporting in terms of value thresholds, industry sector codes and contract confidentiality. For further information please contact the AusTender Help Desk at [tenders@finance.gov.au](mailto:tenders@finance.gov.au).

The CN data reflects contractual information reported by entities in accordance with entities' procurement publishing obligations. Please note that the data contained within each file was correct at the time of extraction. Data may change over time as agencies undertake data quality assurance processes or as contract information is varied. The contract values on AusTender represent the total maximum value of each contract over its life, including where contracts span multiple years. AusTender data does not reflect annual expenditure. 
There is a Data Dictionary available for AusTender Contract Notice information which provides a full list of all the Contract Notice dataset field names and explains the data type, whether it is mandatory, and contains a description to provide further context for the data.

New contracts and contract amendments published within the last eighteen (18) months can be found by perusing the weekly [AusTender Contract Notice Export
files](http://data.gov.au/dataset/austender-contract-notice-export/).

Contracts reported on AusTender are categorised under the United Nations Standard Products and Services Code (UNSPSC) which is reviewed and updated periodically. The UNSPSC is selected by an entity when reporting a contract to reflect the primary purpose of the contract. Below is a list of goods and services category codes used by Australian Government agencies to code their open approaches to market and contracts awarded for publication on AusTender. Code numbers starting with the prefixes **43 a Information Technology, Broadcasting and Telecommunications** and **81 a Engineering and Research and Technology Based Services** apply in the main to Information and Communications Technology related contracts, primarily ICT goods and services respectively.

AusTender Contract Notice data is also available as an Application Programming Interface (API) which provides CN data in the [Open Contracting Data Standard](http://standard.open-contracting.org/) (OCDS) schema.

results.name: industry-geochemistry-compilation-pilot-project
results.notes:
Very large volumes of whole-rock geochemistry data are generated by the mineral exploration industry, with much of this data being lodged with State and Territory governments under legislation governing mineral exploration reporting. The motivation for this Pilot Project arises from the recognition that the wealth of geochemical information that is routinely collected and reported by the mineral exploration industry could be even more valuable and more widely used across jurisdictional borders and at national scale if data reporting standards were more uniform across jurisdictions and that common data issues are remediated or removed from the dataset in a transparent and repeatable way.



The Industry Geochemistry Compilation (IGC) Pilot Project is an initiative led by Geoscience Australia and contracted to RSC Global Pty Ltd (AusTender CN4143262) to evaluate the feasibility and value of creating a national coverage, open-file, industry drillhole geochemistry dataset. The Pilot Project ran from March to June 2025 and includes two related projects, Project 1 and Project 2, which were run in parallel.



Project 1 focused on developing a robust and repeatable data structure, and on cleaning and validating geochemical and spatial data, and is delivered as a Western Australia case study in collaboration with the Geological Survey of Western Australia (GSWA). Key outputs from Project 1 include a cleaned and validated compilation of high-quality industry drillhole multi-element geochemical data, along with the workflow for creating this dataset, delivered as modular, efficient, and well-documented Python code.



Project 2 assessed the scope of work for a national scale data compilation, documenting the rationale and business case for the IGC Pilot Project, reviewing each state/territory geological surveys’ industry geochemistry data holdings, and developing a proposed data architecture for the IGC. Recommendations were made for an optimal data structure for industry submissions and a potential workflow to incorporate each geological survey industry geochemistry dataset into a national compilation was presented.

__AusTender Contract Notice ID__ - Text - This is a reference number generated by AusTender when the Contract Notice was reported on AusTender. __Exchange Date__ - Date [DD/MM/YYYY] - The date the contract for sale of the groundwater entitlement was exchanged between the Commonwealth of Australia and the seller.

__Supplier details__ - Text - The name of the seller of the groundwater entitlement as reported on AusTender.

__Management Zone__ - Text - The groundwater management area from which the groundwater entitlement was purchased.

__Contract Value__ - AUD$ - Purchase price of the groundwater entitlement .

__Contract Volume__ - Number - The number of megalitres (nominal) purchased.

__Suburb__ - Text - As recorded for the seller in the contract for sale of the groundwater entitlement between the Commonwealth of Australia and the seller.

__Postcode__ - Number - As recorded for the seller in the contract for sale of the groundwater entitlement between the Commonwealth of Australia and the seller.

__State__ - Text - As recorded for the seller in the contract for sale of the groundwater entitlement between the Commonwealth of Australia and the seller. QLD is Queensland and NSW is New South Wales.

results.author: Parks Australia
results.name: ashmore-reef-marine-park-environmental-assessment-report-2021
results.notes:
Parks Australia commissioned the CSIRO to undertake a survey of selected marine and terrestrial environmental values at Ashmore Reef Marine Park. The field work was undertaken on two trips, 1– 6 May and 14- 22 June 2019. This report presents the findings of that work.

For the terrestrial component, the required elements were to quantify the diversity and abundance of native and non-native plant species, determine the population status and diversity of seabirds and shorebirds on the islands, and to determine the abundance of non-native invasive tropical fire ants. The remit included any evidence of interactions between the tropical fire ants and native fauna, especially birds and turtles. In addition to these required components, non- native geckos and hermit crabs were surveyed for abundance, the latter being native fauna which would likely be most affected by future attempts to eradicate tropical fire ants. Any work on rodents was not included in the project scope.

For the marine component, the required elements were to survey coral reef communities in particular the abundance of key invertebrates which have historically been the subject of illegal fishing and over-exploitation (holothurians, trochus and tridacnid clams), the status (cover and health) of key habitat forming benthic assemblages (corals, macroalgae and seagrass) and evidence of sea snakes. In addition, surveys of fish and shark diversity and abundance were undertaken, and monitoring sites were established for seagrass biomass and productivity measurements. Incidental observations of turtle abundance were also made, and water samples collected from a subset of sites for potential future analysis of eDNA.

This publication was previously hosted on the Australian Marine Parks webpage, this is now hosted here for continuously access.

results.name: west-cape-york-marine-park-final-report
results.notes:
The West Cape York Marine Park (WCYMP) in Queensland is one of eight marine parks in the North Network 
of Australian Marine Parks. Much of its inshore waters lie within Angkamuthi Sea Country, making it a region 
of both ecological and cultural significance. Between 3-12 December 2024, benthic habitats and fish 
communities across the WCYMP and inshore waters were surveyed aboard the MV Tropic Paradise. 
This survey strengthened marine knowledge and collaborative management of the WCYMP through a 
partnership between Angkamuthi Traditional Owners (via the Seven Rivers Aboriginal Corporation), 
TropWATER at James Cook University, the Northern Institute at Charles Darwin University, and Parks 
Australia. 

The survey set out to characterise benthic habitats and demersal fish diversity using underwater 
cameras and baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS), while also building local capacity by training 
Angkamuthi Traditional Owners in survey techniques and fish video analysis. The fieldwork provided the first 
comprehensive baseline survey for the southern WCYMP and re-examined the previously surveyed central 
section to detect changes in benthic condition. Fish surveys expanded substantially on a 2021 pilot study.
In total, 129 benthic habitat sites were assessed using towed video and sled net from Tropic Paradise and 
video camera drops from its two tenders. Of these, 32 sites were within the National Park Zone, 15 in the 
Habitat Protection Zone, and 61 in the Special Purpose Zone, with an additional 21 coastal sites surveyed just 
inshore of the Special Purpose Zone. 
The benthic habitats recorded included seagrass, algal beds, and invertebrate-dominated communities. 

Seagrass was scarce in the WCYMP, occurring at only 6% of sites with very low cover and biomass. Algae 
were far more widespread, while benthic invertebrate communities—including soft corals, sponges, and 
hard corals—were diverse but generally low in cover, with both hard and soft corals contributing only minor 
structural complexity across the park. The low cover of seagrass and corals was consistent with patterns 
observed in 2021. Sled tows collected a diverse assemblage of sessile and motile invertebrates, including 
habitat-forming Porifera (sponges), Urochordata (ascidians), and Cnidaria (hard and soft corals), as well as 
motile Crinoidea (feather stars), Crustacea (crabs and prawns), and Mollusca (gastropods).
A total of 85 BRUVS were deployed across WCYMP zones and habitats. Visibility had a strong influence on
results, with higher fish species richness and abundance recorded at sites with moderate and clear 
conditions. Across the survey, 80 fish species from 36 families were identified, including 9 shark species and 
10 ray and wedgefish species. Trevallies, threadfin bream, and mackerels were the most common families, 
and yellowstripe scad was the most frequently recorded and abundant species. Fisheries species such as 
Spanish mackerel, grass emperor, queenfish, giant catfish, nannygai, cobia, and whiting were observed, 
though typically in low numbers. 

Shark and ray diversity was high, with whaler, hammerhead and zebra 
sharks recorded, along with whiptail stingrays. Species richness averaged 9 species per site (range: 1–22) and 
was highest inshore and in the Special Purpose Zone. Mean total abundance of fish, sharks and rays was 49.0 
± 4.8 individuals per site (range: 1–268). 
This project delivers bilingual spatial data products—including habitat and species distribution maps—to 
support decision-making in Angkamuthi Sea Country by Traditional Owners, the Seven Rivers Aboriginal 
Corporation, and the Commonwealth Government. The habitat and fish data collected will form the 
foundation for a co-designed monitoring and management framework that weaves together Traditional 
Owner values and knowledge with western scientific approaches, ensuring that marine park priorities and 
stewardship reflect both cultural and ecological perspectives.

results.notes:
The Department of Human Services Annual Report (Annual Report) sets out the department’s activities for the financial year with a focus on the department's performance and financial details, amongst other information.   
  
The Annual Report is prepared in accordance with the Requirements for Annual Reports, issued by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.  Under the *Public Service Act 1999*  (Cth.) the Secretary of the Department of Human Services is required, after the end of each financial year, to provide a report on the department's activities to the Minister, for presentation to the Parliament. Annual Reports are tabled in parliament usually in late October and are available to the public online shortly after tabling.  
  
Reports prior to 2012-2013 can be found on the [Department of Human Services website] (http://www.humanservices.gov.au/corporate/publications-and-resources/annual-report/). 

If you require statistics at a more detailed level, please contact statistics@humanservices.gov.au. The department charges on a cost recovery basis for providing more detailed statistics and their provision is subject to privacy considerations.

This data is provided by the Department of Human Services (Human Services) for general information purposes only. While Human Services has taken care to ensure the information is as correct and accurate as possible, we do not guarantee, or accept legal liability whatsoever arising from, or connected to its use.  
  
We recommend that users exercise their own skill and care with respect to the use of this data and that users carefully evaluate the accuracy, currency, completeness and relevance of the data for their needs.
